A format for storing a sceptre analysis on disk: the settings, the gRNA
assignments, the quality control and the results, stage by stage. It stores
exactly what sceptre, the R package, computes today (version 0.99.1): the same
stages, the same settings under the same names, and the same columns in the
results. An analysis written by sceptre can then be read, checked and
continued by pysceptre (the Python package) or by the Nextflow pipeline, and
the other way round.

An analysis is one folder, and it is an analysis of one data file in the
[Perturb-seq data file format](../perturb-seq-data-format/overview.qmd),
which this format builds on. The folder holds one small file, `analysis.json`,
that says which data file it belongs to, one subfolder for each stage that has
finished, and a cache of saved model fits. The six stages are sceptre's:
`parameters`, `assignment` and `qc`, in that order, and then the three testing
stages `calibration`, `power` and `discovery`, none of which needs another.
Tables are [Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org) files and records are JSON.
The [example](#example) below is such a folder, opened up.

The rules are in the
[specification](SPEC.md)
and the reasons for each in the
[rationale](RATIONALE.md).
A label such as A12 is a group of rules, the same in both, and A12.2 is one
rule of it. Labels starting with D are rules of the data file format.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Draft.** Anything in the format can still change. No released version of
sceptre or pysceptre reads or writes it yet, and there is no function yet for
saving a `sceptre_object` this way: adopting the format in the packages and
the pipeline is the next phase of the
[roadmap](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/ROADMAP.md).
The code in this folder is a prototype used to test the format.
:::

## Principles

Every choice in the format follows from these eight. Where two of them pull
apart, the earlier one wins. Open one for its reason and what follows from it.
Several are the principles of the data file format, applied to an analysis
folder.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.principles("RATIONALE.md", "## The principles"))
```

## Choices made

The main choices beyond the principles. Each opens to its reason and, where there
was one, the alternative it was chosen over.

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>An analysis names its data file by identifier.</strong> <span class="where">A1</span></summary>

- **The choice.** `analysis.json` records the data file's `dataset_id`, its numbers of cells, responses and gRNAs, a hash of each list of identifiers, the data file format's version, and which modality is the response. Software refuses a data file for which the identifier, counts or hashes differ.
- **Why.** The data file can then be moved, copied or kept on a server, and an analysis still knows whether it is being given the right one.
- **A consequence.** A subset of a data file is a different data file, and an analysis of the whole is refused on it.
- **Not caught.** A value edited in place in a data file whose identifiers are unchanged.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The analysis says which modality it tests.</strong> <span class="where">A1</span></summary>

- **The choice.** `analysis.json` names the response modality. Nothing finds it by a fixed name, and the data file marks none.
- **Why.** Any measured modality of a data file can be the response of an analysis: RNA in one, protein in another.
- **Instead of.** A fixed role name such as `response`, which is what both packages use in memory today.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>One folder per stage, with a record written last.</strong> <span class="where">A2</span></summary>

- **The choice.** Each completed stage has a folder holding its tables and `record.json`: the stage's settings, provenance and list of files. The record is written after the tables.
- **Why.** No file is ever rewritten. The record marks the stage as finished, so a folder without one is a stage that did not finish. Calibration, power and discovery do not depend on one another and could run at once without racing for one file. Rerunning a stage is deleting its folder.
- **Instead of.** One settings file rewritten by every stage, or tables grouped by kind with stage ownership recorded elsewhere.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Tables name things by identifier and are sorted by key.</strong> <span class="where">A7, A12</span></summary>

- **Why.** Tables then survive subsetting, reordering and being written in pieces by parallel jobs, and there is no question of counting from 0 or from 1.
- **Consequence.** Results are sorted by target and response, not by p-value.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Assignments are a table of (gRNA, cell) rows, not a matrix.</strong> <span class="where">A8</span></summary>

- **Why.** The assignment belongs to an analysis, not to the data. The table is tiny next to the counts, parallel jobs can each write a part, and another tool can hand in a plain two-column table. A table of 10 million rows reads in about 8 seconds in Python and 10 in R.
- **Instead of.** A 0/1 cells × gRNAs matrix in the data file, which is what the IGVF consortium's pipeline, pertpy (the perturbation package of the Python single-cell ecosystem) and pysceptre use. The two hold the same information.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Low or high multiplicity of infection is a setting of the analysis.</strong> <span class="where">A3</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The parameters record has `moi`, `high` or `low`. The data file does not.
- **Why.** It selects an analysis's defaults, such as the control group and what is done with cells that carry several gRNAs. The same data can be analysed either way.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Covariate names carry the modality's name: <code>rna_n_umis</code>, not <code>response_n_umis</code>.</strong> <span class="where">A14</span></summary>

- **The choice.** A model's covariate table is the data file's shared cell table together with the cell tables of `grna` and of the response modality, each modality's columns prefixed with its name. Formulas use these names.
- **Why.** A role prefix cannot name the RNA depth in an analysis whose response is protein.
- **Cost.** Formulas users write today say `response_n_umis`. The packages would have to keep accepting that name and translate it.
- **Not renamed.** Names of settings keep the role word, as in `response_n_umis_range`: a setting is about the response whatever was measured.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>An analysis can bring covariates of its own.</strong> <span class="where">A14</span></summary>

- **The choice.** An optional table, `parameters/cell_covariates.parquet`, with one row per cell and one column per covariate. A formula may name its columns beside the data file's.
- **Why.** The data file holds nothing a method computed, so a cell-cycle score, a cluster or a cell-type label is kept here. The table also carries the count summaries when a data file does not store them.
- **The rule.** Every covariate of a formula is found in exactly one place: the data file or this table.
- **Kinds.** A covariate here is a number or text. In a data file a text covariate is stored as a categorical; in a Parquet table plain text is read correctly by both languages.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The design matrix is not stored, and formulas are additive only.</strong> <span class="where">A14</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The parameters record holds the formula text and the names of the matrix's columns. Each language rebuilds the matrix and checks those names.
- **What is checked.** The names of the matrix's columns, such as `batchbatch_2`, which carry the factor levels, the baseline level and the order of terms. A reader that rebuilds the matrix and gets other names refuses the analysis.
- **Evidence.** On the example, R and pysceptre build matrices that are equal to the last bit on one machine.
- **Cost.** Only additive formulas of covariates, `log(x)` and `log(x + 1)` can be saved. An analysis with an interaction or a spline cannot be.
- **No hash of the matrix.** A hash of exact values would fail on a correct matrix, because a logarithm's last bit differs between macOS and Linux (measured). A check that survives this can be added later.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Saved model fits are a cache outside the stages.</strong> <span class="where">A13</span></summary>

- **The choice.** `fits/response/` holds part files. Each part says, inside the file, how its fits were made, and software uses a part only when that matches what it would do itself. Deleting the folder changes no result beyond rounding: a fit that is not found is fitted again by the same routine.
- **Why.** A fit depends on the data, the formula, the control group and the cells that passed QC, all fixed once QC has run. Which testing stage computes it first is an accident, so a stage's folder is the wrong home: rerunning that stage would delete fits that are still valid.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The <code>significant</code> column is not stored.</strong> <span class="where">A12</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The records of the calibration and discovery stages have the largest p-value that was called significant, and a pair is significant when its p-value is at most that. The threshold is `null` when no pair was called significant.
- **Why.** Significance depends on every pair of the stage, and a table written in parts by parallel jobs cannot hold a column that needs the whole table.
- **Also.** A pair that failed quality control keeps its row, with `pass_qc` false and no p-value.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Whether a table is per target or per gRNA follows from the strategy.</strong> <span class="where">A10, A12</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The pair and results tables have a `grna_id` column when they are per gRNA and not when they are per target. Under `union` none has it, and under `singleton` all do. Under `bonferroni` the pair-quality-control tables and the calibration results have it, and the power and discovery results do not.
- **Why.** It is how sceptre reports its results, and software then knows a table's key without opening it.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>A table can be a folder of part files.</strong> <span class="where">A7</span></summary>

- **The choice.** A table is one file or a folder of part files with the same columns. Each parallel job writes a part of its own, under a name of its choosing, and nothing is gathered into one file afterwards. The stage's record, written last, lists the table and its total number of rows.
- **Not tried yet.** No pipeline has written part files. Whether this fits how the Nextflow pipeline splits and gathers its work is open.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong><code>B3</code> is recorded wherever sceptre may change it.</strong> <span class="where">A3</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The resampling budget `B3` is in the records of `parameters`, `qc` and `calibration`, and the value in the latest record that has one is in force.
- **Why.** In sceptre, `run_qc()` and `run_calibration_check()` may each change it, so the budget a testing stage uses depends on which functions were called before it.
- **Instead of.** Each testing stage recording the value it used.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Resampled statistics are stored as 64-bit numbers.</strong> <span class="where">A12</span></summary>

- **The choice.** `resamples.parquet` holds one list per pair, 499 values or more, as sceptre computes them.
- **Instead of.** 32-bit numbers, at half the size.

</details>

## Example

The tree below is a real analysis folder,
`example/highmoi/analyses/left_sided/`: a left-sided analysis of sceptre's
high-MOI example data. It was computed by sceptre 0.99.1, and its
`sceptre_object` was then written out with the prototype writer in `format/`.
Open a folder to see its
files, and a file to see its first rows or its contents. The descriptions are
read from the specification's own files.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(at.analysis_tree())
```

This analysis has no `cell_covariates.parquet` and no `resamples.parquet`,
which are optional, and it uses the `union` strategy, so its tables have no
`grna_id`. Seven more example analyses are in `example/`, among them one under
the `singleton` strategy, one that assigned gRNAs with the `mixture` method,
one of sceptre's low-MOI example data, one that stopped after quality
control, and one that kept its resampled statistics.

## Reading

A data file and an analysis folder are read together into the object sceptre
itself works with. In R that is a `sceptre_object` of sceptre 0.99.1, complete:
every function of the package that takes one works on it.

```{r}
#| include: false
source("sceptre-suite/setup.R")
```

```{r}
data_file <- "../perturb-seq-data-format/example/highmoi/screen.h5mu"
analysis <- read_sceptre_object(data_file, "example/highmoi/analyses/left_sided")
print(analysis)
```

No package is needed to read the files themselves. The tables are Parquet and
the records are JSON, so any tool that reads those can use an analysis without
sceptre.

## Writing

A `sceptre_object` is written as an analysis folder beside its data file, with
one subfolder for each stage that has been run. Here the object read above is
written to a new folder, which the validator then finds no fault with.

```{r}
folder <- file.path(tempdir(), "my_analysis")
write_sceptre_object(analysis, data_file, folder)
list.files(folder, recursive = TRUE)
nrow(validate_analysis(folder, data_file))    # the number of rules broken
```

The reader and the writer here are prototypes, in `sceptre-suite/`, and are
meant to become functions of the sceptre package. pysceptre will read and
write the same folders with its own object; no version of it does yet.

## Validation

Five things check the format: a validator, a set of test folders, a suite of
checks that uses no package, a second suite that uses sceptre, and automatic
runs of both on every change.

### What "conforms" means

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"""The specification has {counts["all"]} numbered statements of three kinds.

| Kind | What it is about | How many | How it is checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| File rule | What a folder contains | {counts["file"]} | By the validator. The validators check {counts["file_checked"]} of them |
| Behaviour rule | What software reading or writing a folder does | {counts["behaviour"]} | By a test where one exists: {counts["behaviour_tested"]} have one |
| Guidance | Advice to whoever writes analyses | {counts["guidance"]} | Not checked |
""")
```

A folder **conforms** when it breaks no file rule. `SPEC.md` says beside each
statement how it is checked, and which ones nothing tests yet. Several
behaviour rules say what a package that fits models must do, and can only be
tested once sceptre and pysceptre read and write these files.

### The validator

`validate_analysis()` takes an analysis folder, and optionally its data file,
and returns the rules it breaks, with where and why. It exists twice, in R and
in Python (`format/`), and both read the same machine-readable definitions
(`spec/`). It runs without sceptre or pysceptre installed.

Without the data file it checks the folder on its own: the records, the
tables, their columns, types and order. With the data file it also checks
what ties the two together: that it is the right data file, that every cell,
gRNA and response named in a table exists in it, and that every covariate the
formula names can be found. Here it is on a test folder whose formula names
covariates that neither the data file nor the analysis provides:

```{python}
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "format")
import sceptre_analysis

problems = sceptre_analysis.validate_analysis(
    "conformance/invalid/analyses/formula_names_an_unknown_covariate",
    "../perturb-seq-data-format/conformance/valid/highmoi_without_count_summaries.h5mu")
print(problems.to_string(index=False))
```

On a conforming folder the result is empty.

### The conformance folders

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"""`conformance/` holds {conforming} cases that conform and {broken} that each break
one rule or a few. A case is an analysis folder together with the data file
it is checked against. `conformance/cases.json` says, for every case, which
rules a validator must report. Both validators must report exactly those, no
more and no fewer. Someone writing another implementation tests it against the
same cases.""")
```

### The suite

`verify/run.sh` runs every check, in R and in Python, and prints a summary. The counts below are from the run
this page was rendered after.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.status({
    "conformance": "Both validators report exactly the expected rules on every conformance case",
    "independent-readers": "Tools that know nothing of this format read the example tables: pandas, polars and duckdb in Python; arrow in R",
    "encodings": "Every kind of table column, written by each language's standard Parquet library and read by the other's",
    "derived": "What software works out from the files (cells per gRNA and per target, cells in use, pairs passing quality control, significance, control groups) equals what sceptre computed for the same analysis. sceptre's values were recorded once, in `example/*/expected/`, and the check compares against that record",
    "two-writers": "R and Python each write the same random content, a data file and an analysis of it. The files are compared value by value, and each language reads the other's files and gets the content back",
    "writers": "What a writer must do beyond producing a conforming folder: a stage written again after a failed attempt leaves nothing of the first attempt",
}))
```

- The two languages run different numbers of checks in some groups, because
  each tests its own libraries.
- The first four groups use no writer: they check the validators and standard
  libraries against files already in the repository. The last two check the
  prototype writers in `format/`. When sceptre and pysceptre write these
  files themselves, the same two groups will check the packages' files
  instead.

### The sceptre suite

The validator and the suite above deliberately use neither package: a folder
must be checkable wherever it is, whoever wrote it. But the format also claims
to hold exactly what a sceptre analysis holds, and only sceptre can test that.
`sceptre-suite/run.sh` installs nothing itself and needs sceptre 0.99.1. It
has sceptre run the eight example analyses again, and then checks three
things for each:

- **The examples are what sceptre produces.** The folder written from
  sceptre's object conforms, and equals the example in the repository.
- **Nothing is lost.** A `sceptre_object` rebuilt from the data file and the
  folder alone equals the object the folder was written from, slot by slot.
  Two slots are left out, `M_matrix` and `n_nonzero_tot_vector`, which sceptre
  computes again from the data.
- **The settings are complete.** sceptre, run again from only the settings in
  the records, gives the same results.

If sceptre's output and the format drift apart, this suite fails.

### Automatic runs

The suite runs by itself on GitHub whenever a change is pushed to this folder
or to the data file format's folder, since this format depends on that one. It
runs on three fresh machines: Linux, macOS and Windows. Each installs only
standard libraries, then runs `verify/run.sh`. A fourth machine installs
sceptre 0.99.1 and runs the sceptre suite. A failure on any of them marks the
change as failing. The current state and the history of runs are at the
[workflow's page](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/actions/workflows/sceptre-analysis-format.yml).

### At real size

The example analyses are small: 500 or 1,000 cells. Once, by hand, the tables
were written and read at the size of a large screen, with made-up content
(`scale-test/`).

- **Results tables** are no problem: 100 million pairs take 2.5 GB, and one
  pair is read in a tenth of a second.
- **Resampled statistics** are large: 4 GB per million pairs. A Parquet file
  is written in blocks of rows, and reading one pair means reading its whole
  block: a tenth of a second with blocks of 10,000 rows, 7 seconds with
  blocks of a million. The format therefore limits a block of this table to
  10,000 rows.
- **Saved fits** take time to read in proportion to the number of part
  files: 10,000 parts take a minute and a half. The format therefore advises
  one part per job, and allows parts to be merged once no job is writing.
